newsitem.title: USA: U.S. delegation head sees industry e-commerce role.
newsitem.headline: U.S. delegation head sees industry e-commerce role.

text.p: A U.S. trade policy delegation head said on Thursday President Bill Clinton will next week include a major role for high technology leaders when he unveils U.S. electronic commerce policy.

James Johnson, who heads the U.S. delegation to the Group of Seven major industrial powers' electronic commerce policy group, told industry executives here the White House will put forward its policy on July 1.

The adminstration has posted a draft copy of its "Framework for Global Electronic Commerce" on the World Wide Web earlier this year, and Johnson said the final version will include many of the key proposals put forward in the original draft.
These include maintaining the Internet as a non-taxable, duty free zone, he said.

Johnson said the administration will reason that it is difficult to track what boundaries apply to commerce conducted in cyberspace, and that the history of much of this century has been an effort to reduce global tariffs.
"The U.S. is going to argue: why start taxing trade on the Internet," he said in a keynote address to Giga Information Group's Business OnLine 97 symposium here.

The Clinton administration would make this a key element in an "agenda for action," which it intends to put forward on a worldwide basis and use in its negotiations for global standards for the worldwide computer network.

On Tuesday, a resolution of the U.S. Conference of Mayors, meeting in San Francisco, opposed federal legislation to prevent state and local governments from slapping new taxes on Internet transactions.
The resolution, which passed without debate, urged the Clinton administration and Congress to delay taking action on the issue until "thorough and impartial" studies were completed.

Public policy surrounding the Internet was brought to the forefront again on Thursday as the U.S. Supreme Court struck down a federal law that severely restricted indecent pictures and words on the Internet.
Johnson said the administration considered it critical to seek the involvement of the computer industry in setting out standards for electronic commerce.

These include complex issues of security and use of cryptography on which the industry and the U.S. government have been at odds recently, with computer companies arguing that World War II era laws defining use of strong cryptography as restricted munitions are outdated.
The Clinton administration has shown increasing signs of flexibility on this matter, despite continued concerns that cryptography could be used by terrorists and criminals.
Netscape Communications Corp. and Microsoft Corp. said this week they were granted permission to export products with strong encryption for use by banks and the financial industry.
